title: Executive Thesis, Dual Verdict & Opportunity Matrix
web_title: 0. Executive Thesis, Dual Verdict & Opportunity Matrix
question: What does Greaves Cotton make, what does the price require, and what should you do now?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, 2008

web_blocks.takeaway: The business is investable but not at this price. Because the account owns no Greaves shares, the new-money and holding questions have the same answer: do nothing today and let the price come to us [108][118].

web_blocks.text: Greaves Cotton has three parts. The core makes diesel engines, gensets (engines coupled to alternators), vehicle control cables and aftermarket parts. In H1 FY27 it earned ₹1,478 crore of revenue, up 20%, at an operating profit (EBITDA) margin of 12.0%, down from 14.9% a year earlier as metal costs outran customer repricing [1][24]. Greaves Electric Mobility Limited (GEML), 62.5% owned, sells Ampere scooters and L5 three-wheelers. Its revenue doubled to ₹680 crore, and it lost ₹63 crore at EBITDA [1]. Greaves Finance lends against electric vehicles and managed ₹630 crore of assets [1]. The core earns the profit and GEML consumes capital: group operating cash flow was −₹212 crore in H1 FY27, and borrowings reached ₹513 crore against ₹606 crore of cash and investments, after a ₹530 crore rights issue [2][62].

At ₹225.97 the market values the whole group at about ₹5,226 crore of enterprise value, or 20.1 times trailing EBITDA [109][118]. Our reverse DCF, which solves for the growth that justifies today's price, says it needs about 12.5% revenue growth a year for ten years while group margin climbs from 6.5% to 12%. Greaves has grown about 6.6% a year over eleven years and last earned a 12% group margin in FY19 [118]. Our sum-of-the-parts value is ₹303 in the base case, ₹427 in the bull case and ₹152 in the bear case. Weighted 45%, 25% and 30%, that is ₹288.7, or 27.8% above the close and about 13% a year over two years [118]. A more conservative cross-check on earnings gives a base near ₹273, which would cut the return to about 10% a year, below our 12% hurdle.

The bull argument is that the core held 13–14% margins for three years, medium-horsepower gensets grew 35% and auto engines 37%, the loss per scooter shrank from about ₹20,000 to ₹6,300, and the rights issue funds GEML for 12–18 months [1][62]. The bear argument is that margin is falling while revenue grows, the group has produced negative operating cash flow, GEML has no dated breakeven, and FAME-II showed that subsidy rules can cut volume 56% in a year [24][2]. We weight the bear slightly above the bull because the turn in cash has no date in any filing.

Short term, we do not buy at ₹225.97 after an 11% weekly rise, with supply overhead between ₹230 and ₹272 [108]. Medium term, the odds are good only from a lower price. Long term, gensets, engines and cables can compound, but GEML absorbs capital and the group earns a 10.1% ROCE. Execution is exact. We would begin an entry review inside ₹205.02–₹211.26, around the 10-week average of ₹208.14, and buy only if the KPI alerts are clear. A daily close below ₹197.60 cancels the idea. A daily close above ₹271.90 on rising volume, with Q3 FY27 core margin of 13% or more, starts an upgrade review. Two more quarters of negative operating cash flow, or another GEML funding round, would move the verdict to REJECTED [108][118].

The dual verdict is plain. New capital: WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT. Current holding: NOT_HELD, with 0 shares to sell. The next marginal cash unit goes 100% to cash, 0% to AJMERA (₹133.28, just above its ₹124.51–₹132.17 zone) and 0% to GREAVESCOT. Support-zone asymmetry, base reward divided by stop risk, is 6.7:1, but cash flow and extension keep us out for now [118].

web_blocks.title: Gate exceptions in plain English
paragraphs: The status is PUBLISHED_WITH_GATE_EXCEPTIONS. First, the market-facts ledger and the TradingView snapshot are one bar apart: the ledger holds the 12 November close of ₹223.18, the snapshot the 13 November close of ₹225.97, and we use the newer figure for levels. Second, TheWrap's Stage 2 dashboard is dated 8 November and does not list Greaves, so the Stage 2 label rests on our own moving-average evidence, not independent leadership confirmation [110]. Third, Greaves is not optionable, so this is a cash-equity decision only [117].

book_paragraphs: Picture a quiet Friday evening. The market has closed, the chart shows ₹225.97, and you are wondering whether to act. Before we answer, let me ask the question I always ask first: what does this company actually do? Greaves Cotton makes engines. Some power diesel three-wheelers, some are bolted to alternators to make generators for hospitals and factories, and some sit inside fire pumps. It also makes the push-pull cables that run throttles and gear levers. That is the part that earns money, and it has done so for years.

Next to it sits a younger business, Greaves Electric Mobility, which makes the Ampere scooter. Here the picture reverses. Sales have doubled in six months, which looks wonderful, yet the unit still loses money at the operating line. A scooter that lost about twenty thousand rupees a year ago now loses about sixty-three hundred. That is real progress, and still a loss. A small finance arm lends to buyers of electric vehicles, and its book grows in step with the scooters.

So the group is two stories in one wrapper. The old engine business grew twenty percent in the half year but kept less of each rupee, because aluminium, iron and copper got dearer before customers agreed to pay more. The scooter business grew faster and asked for cash. In the first half of this year the whole group took in less cash from operations than it spent, by about two hundred and twelve crore rupees. Management raised five hundred and thirty crore in a rights issue so the scooter company can keep going for a year or more. You and I should respect that fix and still ask the harder question about when the cash turns.

Now, what is the price asking you to believe? Imagine the share price as a bill at the end of a long dinner. We work backward and ask what kind of evening would justify it. The answer is that Greaves would need to grow sales by roughly twelve and a half percent every year for a decade, while its overall profit margin climbs to twelve percent. The company has grown about half that fast over eleven years, and it last earned such a margin years ago. That does not make the price absurd. It means the price expects a recovery, and recoveries are never free.

Because the business has two halves, we valued each on its own terms. We built three pictures of November 2028. In the good picture the engine margin recovers fully and the market pays a generous multiple, giving four hundred and twenty-seven rupees a share. In the middle picture the margin climbs back to thirteen and a half percent, giving three hundred and three. In the poor picture margins stay squeezed and the scooter company asks its parent for another hundred and fifty crore, giving one hundred and fifty-two. We gave those pictures odds of one in four, nearly one in two and about one in three, and the weighted answer was two hundred and eighty-nine.

That is about twenty-eight percent above today's price over two years, roughly thirteen percent a year. It sounds comfortable until you notice how little room it leaves. Our hurdle is twelve percent a year. A slightly sterner way of valuing the same business pulls the return under eleven. Buy at today's price and you are paid just enough if everything goes to plan, and not enough if one assumption slips. Now imagine paying around two hundred and eight rupees instead. The same value then gives you about eighteen percent a year. You did not need a better forecast. You needed a better entry.

That is why the verdict is to wait for support, and why I want you to hear it as an instruction rather than a shrug. The zone runs from two hundred and five to two hundred and eleven rupees. If the stock closes below one hundred and ninety-eight, we drop the idea. If it instead closes above two hundred and seventy-two, its old high, with strong volume and a better margin in the next quarterly result, we reopen the case and review the verdict. Notice that each of these is a number you can look up, not a mood.

What about what you already own? In this account, nothing. The ledger shows no Greaves shares, so there is nothing to hold, trim or sell, and no reason to buy a few shares just to feel involved. The next fresh rupee stays in cash. One shortlist name, Ajmera, looks cheaper and has better reward for risk, but it also sits just above its own zone. Patience applies to both. The portfolio already holds a lot of similar auto and industrial cyclicals, so even a good Greaves entry would be small.

I also owe you three honest confessions about the evidence. The market-facts ledger carries the twelfth of November close while the live snapshot carries the thirteenth, one bar newer, so a few figures differ by a day. A weekly leadership dashboard dated the eighth does not list Greaves among its rising stocks, so the chart is our only confirmation of strength. And the stock cannot be traded in options. None of this changes the verdict. All of it is why we publish with these exceptions stated, not hidden.

Over six months, then, do not chase. Over two years, the odds are good from a lower price and merely adequate from here. Over five years, this is a decent cyclical engine business, not yet a compounder, because the group still earns about ten percent on the capital it employs. If you carry one sentence away, make it this. A good business is not a good purchase at every price, and writing down your price, your stop and the facts that would change your mind is what turns a view into a decision.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Price is what you pay and value is what you get. The distance between them is the only margin of safety you can measure, so write the number down before the market tempts you to forget it.
